blocks.p: But after consulting among themselves, and with some of their captains, they went once more to the Lord Secretary for advice. For the Lord Secretary was their chief preacher, as I mentioned some pages back; only now he was ill at ease. They begged his favor in two or three things.

1. First, that he would look on them kindly, and not keep himself so withdrawn from them as before; and that he would give them a hearing while they laid their miserable condition before him. But to this he told them, as before, “that as yet he was ill at ease, and therefore could not do as he had formerly done.”

2. Second, that he would advise them in their present weighty affairs, for Diabolus had come and sat down before the town with no fewer than twenty thousand Doubters. Both he and his captains, they said, were cruel men, and they were afraid of them. But to this he said, “You must look to the law of the Prince, and see there what it lays on you to do.”

3. Third, they asked that His Highness would help them frame a petition to Shaddai, and to Emmanuel his Son, and that he would set his own hand to it as a sign that he was one with them in it. “For, my Lord,” they said, “we have sent many a petition, and can get no answer of peace; but surely one with your hand to it may obtain good for Mansoul.”
But all the answer he gave to this was “that they had offended their Emmanuel, and had grieved him too, and that therefore they must for now live with the fruit of their own devices.”

This answer fell on them like a millstone. It crushed them so that they did not know what to do; and yet they did not dare give in to the demands of Diabolus or of his captain. Here, then, was the narrow place the town of Mansoul was caught in when the enemy came against her: her foes were ready to swallow her up, and her friends held back from helping her.

Then the Lord Mayor, whose name was my Lord Understanding, stood up and began to pick and pick at that seemingly bitter saying of the Lord Secretary’s until he had picked some comfort out of it. “First,” he said, “it follows unavoidably from what my Lord said that we must yet suffer for our sins. But second, the words still sound as if at last we shall be saved from our enemies, and as if, after a few more sorrows, Emmanuel will come and be our help.” Now the Lord Mayor weighed the Secretary’s words the more carefully because my Lord was more than a prophet, and every word of his always meant exactly what it said; and the townsmen were allowed to search into them and draw from them all the good they could.

So they took their leave of my Lord and told the captains what my Lord High Secretary had said; and the captains were all of the same opinion as the Lord Mayor. So they began to take courage, and to prepare to make some brave attack on the enemy’s camp, and to destroy all the Diabolonians, along with the roving Doubters the tyrant had brought with him to destroy the poor town of Mansoul.

So everyone went at once to his post: the captains to theirs, the Lord Mayor to his, the town’s own preacher to his, and my Lord Willbewill to his. The captains longed to be at some work for their Prince, for they delighted in deeds of war. The next day, therefore, they met in council and resolved to give the captain of Diabolus his answer with their slings. And so they did, at sunrise the next morning; for Diabolus had ventured to come nearer again, but the sling-stones were like hornets to him and his. For as nothing is so terrible to the town of Mansoul as the roaring of Diabolus’s drum, so nothing is so terrible to Diabolus as the well-played slings of Emmanuel. So Diabolus was forced to retreat still farther from the famous town of Mansoul. Then the Lord Mayor had the bells rung, and gave orders “that thanks be sent to the Lord High Secretary by the mouth of the town’s own preacher, because by his words the captains and elders of Mansoul had been strengthened against Diabolus.”

When Diabolus saw his captains and soldiers, high and renowned lords, frightened and beaten down by the stones from the golden slings of the Prince of Mansoul, he thought it over and said, “I will try to catch them by fawning. I will try to flatter them into my net.”

So after a while he came down to the wall again, not with his drum this time, nor with Captain Sepulchre; but with his lips all sugared over, he seemed a very sweet-spoken, peaceable prince, who wanted nothing for his own pleasure’s sake, and had no wish to be revenged on Mansoul for the injuries they had done him. The welfare, good, and advantage of the town and its people were now, he said, his only aim. So, having called for a hearing, he began his speech:

“Oh, my heart’s desire, famous town of Mansoul! How many nights have I lain awake, and how many weary steps have I taken, if only I might do you good! Far be it, far be it from me to want to make war on you, if you will only give yourselves up to me willingly and quietly. You know you were mine of old. Remember, too, that as long as you had me for your lord and I had you for my subjects, you lacked nothing of all the delights of the earth that I, your lord and prince, could get for you, or could invent to make you merry and glad. Think about it: you never had so many hard, dark, troubled, heart-sore hours while you were mine as you have had since you revolted from me; nor will you ever have peace again until you and I are one, as before. Only be persuaded to embrace me again, and I will grant your old charter, yes, and enlarge it, with privileges in abundance, so that you shall have license and liberty to take, hold, enjoy, and make your own whatever is pleasant from the east to the west. Nor will I ever hold against you any of the discourtesies by which you have offended me, as long as the sun and moon endure. Nor shall any of those dear friends of mine who now, for fear of you, lie lurking in dens and holes and caves in Mansoul ever hurt you again. No, they shall be your servants, and shall supply you out of their own goods and out of whatever else comes to hand. I need say no more. You know them, and not long ago you took great delight in their company. Why, then, should we stay at such odds? Let us renew our old acquaintance and friendship.

“Bear with your friend. I speak freely to you now because the love I have for you compels me, and so does the zeal of my heart for my friends among you. So do not put me to further trouble, nor yourselves to further fears and frights. Have you I will, whether by peace or by war. And do not flatter yourselves with the power and strength of your captains, or with the thought that your Emmanuel will soon come to help you; for such strength will do you no good.

“I have come against you with a strong and valiant army, and all the chief princes of the den are at the head of it. Besides, my captains are swifter than eagles, stronger than lions, and greedier for prey than the evening wolves. What is Og of Bashan? What is Goliath of Gath? What are a hundred more like them, compared with the least of my captains? How, then, can Mansoul think to escape my hand and my power?”
When Diabolus had delivered this flattering, fawning, deceitful, and lying speech, the Lord Mayor answered him:

“Diabolus, prince of darkness and master of all deceit, we have tested your lying flatteries enough, and drunk too deeply of that deadly cup already. If we listened to you again, and so broke the commandments of our great Shaddai to join ourselves with you, would not our Prince reject us and cast us off forever? And once cast off by him, could the place he has prepared for you be a place of rest for us? Besides, you who are empty and void of all truth, we would rather die by your hand than fall in with your flattering and lying deceits.”

When the tyrant saw there was little to be gained by parleying with the Lord Mayor, he flew into a hellish rage, and resolved that he would once again assault the town of Mansoul with his army of Doubters.

So he called for his drummer, who beat to summon his men (and while he beat, Mansoul shook) to be ready to give battle to the town. Then Diabolus drew near with his army and placed his men in this way. Captain Cruel and Captain Torment he drew up and placed against Feel-gate, and ordered them to sit down there for the war; and he arranged that, if need be, Captain No-Ease should come to their relief. At Nose-gate he placed Captain Brimstone and Captain Sepulchre, and told them to keep a close watch on that side of the town. But at Eye-gate he placed that grim-faced one, Captain Past-Hope, and there too he now set up his terrible standard.
Captain Insatiable was to look after Diabolus’s baggage train, and to take charge of whatever persons or things might be captured from the enemy as plunder.

Now the people of Mansoul kept Mouth-gate as their sally-port, the gate from which they made their sorties against the enemy, and so they kept it strong; for it was the gate by which the townsfolk sent their petitions out to Emmanuel their Prince. It was also the gate from whose top the captains played their slings on the enemy; for that gate stood somewhat high, so that slings let fly from there did great damage to the tyrant’s army. For these reasons and others, Diabolus tried, if he could, to choke Mouth-gate with dirt.

Now as Diabolus was busy outside preparing his assault, so the captains and soldiers in the town were just as busy preparing within. They mounted their slings, set up their banners, sounded their trumpets, and arranged themselves in whatever order was judged best to harass the enemy and to help Mansoul; and they ordered their soldiers to be ready for war at the sound of the trumpet. Lord Willbewill, for his part, took charge of watching against the rebels within, and of doing what he could to catch them when they ventured out, or to smother them in their caves, dens, and holes in the town wall of Mansoul. And to tell the truth about him, ever since he did penance for his fault he has shown as much honesty and courage of spirit as any man in Mansoul. For he took one Jolly and his brother Giddy, the two sons of his servant Harmless-mirth (for though their father had been committed to prison, the sons were still living in my lord’s house to that day); I say, he took them, and with his own hands he put them to the cross. And this was why he hanged them. After their father was handed over to Mr. True-Man the jailer, his sons began to play their father’s tricks, and to flirt and dally with their lord’s daughters; indeed it was suspected that they had grown too familiar with them, and this came to his lordship’s ear. Now his lordship, unwilling to put any man to death rashly, did not fall on them at once, but set spies to see whether it was true. He soon knew: for his two servants, whose names were Find-Out and Tell-All, caught them together in an indecent manner more than once or twice, and went and told their lord. So when my Lord Willbewill had good grounds to believe it, he took the two young Diabolonians (for such they were, since their father was a Diabolonian born) and brought them to Eye-gate. There he raised a very high cross, right in the face of Diabolus and his army, and there he hanged the young villains, in defiance of Captain Past-Hope and of the tyrant’s horrible standard.

Now this Christian act of the brave Lord Willbewill greatly dismayed Captain Past-Hope. It discouraged the army of Diabolus, put fear into the Diabolonian renegades in Mansoul, and put strength and courage into the captains who belonged to Emmanuel the Prince. For those outside gathered from this very act of my lord’s that Mansoul was resolved to fight, and that the Diabolonians within the town could not do the things Diabolus had hoped they would. Nor was this the only proof of the brave Lord Willbewill’s honesty toward the town and his loyalty to his Prince, as will appear later.

Now Prudent-thrifty, too, had left children behind him with Mr. Mind when he was committed to prison. Their names were Grasp and Rake-All, and he had fathered them on Mr. Mind’s illegitimate daughter, whose name was Mrs. Hold-fast-Bad. When these children saw how Lord Willbewill had dealt with the two who lived with him, what did they do but try to escape, for fear they would drink from the same cup? But Mr. Mind was on his guard, and caught them, and kept them locked up in his house until morning (for this happened at night). Then, remembering that by the law of Mansoul all Diabolonians were to die (and they certainly were Diabolonians on their father’s side at least, and some say on their mother’s side too), what did he do but put them in chains and carry them to the very place where my lord had hanged his two before; and there he hanged them.

The townsmen took great encouragement from this, and did what they could to catch more of these Diabolonian troublers. But at that time the rest lay so low and so close that they could not be taken. So they set a careful watch against them, and every man went to his post.

I told you a little earlier that Diabolus and his army were somewhat dismayed at what my Lord Willbewill did when he hanged those two young Diabolonians. But his discouragement soon turned into furious madness and rage against the town of Mansoul, and fight it he would. The townsmen and captains within, meanwhile, had their hopes raised, believing the day would be theirs at last, so they feared the enemy less. Their own preacher, too, preached a sermon on it, and took this for his text: “Gad, a troop shall overcome him, but he shall overcome at the last.” [Gen. 49:19] From it he showed that though Mansoul would be hard pressed at first, yet the victory would most certainly be Mansoul’s in the end.

So Diabolus commanded his drummer to beat a charge against the town; and the captains in the town sounded a charge against them too, though they had no drum: they had trumpets of silver, and with these they sounded against them. Then the soldiers of Diabolus’s camp came down to the town to take it, and the captains in the castle, with the slingers at Mouth-gate, poured their shot on them with all their might. And now nothing was heard in the camp of Diabolus but horrible rage and blasphemy; but in the town, good words, prayer, and the singing of psalms. The enemy answered with horrible objections and the terror of their drum; but the town replied with the slapping of their slings and the music of their trumpets. And so the fight went on for several days, with only a short break now and then for the townsmen to refresh themselves and the captains to make ready for another assault.

The captains of Emmanuel were clothed in silver armor, and the soldiers in armor of proof, that no blow could pierce; the soldiers of Diabolus were clothed in iron, which was made to give way before the shot of Emmanuel’s engines. In the town some were hurt, and some badly wounded. And the worst of it was that a surgeon was hard to find in Mansoul, since Emmanuel was absent for now. Still, the wounded were kept from dying with the leaves of a tree; yet their wounds festered badly, and some of them stank grievously. Of the townsmen these were wounded: my Lord Reason, who was wounded in the head; the brave Lord Mayor, who was wounded in the eye; Mr. Mind, who received his wound about the stomach; and that honest man, the town’s own preacher, who took a shot not far from the heart. But none of these wounds was mortal.
Many of the common sort, too, were not only wounded but killed outright.

In the camp of Diabolus also a considerable number were wounded and killed. Captain Rage, for instance, was wounded, and so was Captain Cruel. Captain Damnation was forced to retreat and dig himself in farther off from Mansoul. Diabolus’s standard was beaten down as well, and his standard-bearer, Captain Much-Hurt, had his brains dashed out with a sling-stone, to the no small grief and shame of his prince Diabolus.

Many of the Doubters, too, were killed outright, though enough of them were left alive to make Mansoul shake and totter. The victory that day put great courage into the townsmen and captains, and covered Diabolus’s camp with a cloud; but it also made them far more furious. So the next day Mansoul rested, and ordered the bells to be rung; the trumpets sounded joyfully too, and the captains shouted all around the town.

My Lord Willbewill was not idle either, but did notable service within against the Diabolonians in the town, and not only by keeping them in awe. For at last he lighted on one whose name was Mr. Any-side, a fellow I mentioned before: it was he, if you remember, who brought to Diabolus the three fellows whom the Diabolonians had taken out of Captain Boanerges’s companies, and who persuaded them to enlist under the tyrant and fight against the army of Shaddai. My Lord Willbewill also took a notable Diabolonian named Loose-Foot. This Loose-Foot was a scout for the vagabonds in Mansoul, and used to carry news out of Mansoul to the camp, and out of the camp to the enemies in Mansoul. My lord sent both of these safely away to Mr. True-Man, the jailer, with orders to keep them in irons; for he intended to bring them out to be crucified when it would be best for the town and most discouraging to the enemy’s camp.

My Lord Mayor, too, though he could not move about as much as before because of the wound he had lately received, yet gave orders to all the natives of Mansoul to keep their watch, to stand on their guard, and, as occasion offered, to prove themselves men.
Mr. Conscience, the preacher, also did his utmost to keep all his good teaching alive in the hearts of the people of Mansoul.

Well, a while later the captains and bold spirits of Mansoul settled on a time to make a sally against the camp of Diabolus; and this was to be done at night. And there was the folly of Mansoul; for the night is always best for the enemy and worst for Mansoul to fight in. Yet they would do it, their courage was so high, and their last victory still stuck in their memories.

So when the appointed night came, the Prince’s brave captains cast lots to decide who should lead the van in this new and desperate expedition against Diabolus and his Diabolonian army; and the lot fell to Captain Credence, Captain Experience, and Captain Good-Hope to lead the forlorn hope, the advance party that goes first into the greatest danger. (This Captain Experience the Prince had commissioned when he himself was living in the town of Mansoul.) So, as I said, they sallied out against the army that lay besieging them; and as it happened, they fell in with the main body of their enemies. Now Diabolus and his men, being well practiced in night work, took the alarm at once, and were as ready to give them battle as if they had been sent word of their coming. So at it they went with all their might, and the blows fell hard on every side. The drum of hell was beaten most furiously, while the trumpets of the Prince sounded most sweetly. And so the battle was joined; and Captain Insatiable kept watch over the enemy’s baggage, waiting for the time when he should receive some plunder.

The Prince’s captains fought bravely, beyond what anyone could have expected of them. They wounded many, and drove the whole army of Diabolus into retreat. But I cannot tell how it happened: as the brave Captain Credence, Captain Good-Hope, and Captain Experience were in pursuit, cutting the enemy down and following hard on their rear, Captain Credence stumbled and fell, and was so badly hurt by the fall that he could not get up until Captain Experience helped him to his feet; and at this their men fell into disorder. The captain, too, was in such pain that he could not keep from crying out aloud. At this the other two captains lost heart, supposing that Captain Credence had received his death wound; and their men were thrown into greater disorder still, and had no heart left to fight. Now Diabolus was very watchful; and though at this point he was still getting the worst of it, he noticed that the men pursuing him had come to a halt. What did he do but take it for granted that the captains were either wounded or dead? So first he made a stand, then turned about, and came down on the Prince’s army with as much fury as hell could lend him. And as it happened, he fell right in among the three captains, Captain Credence, Captain Good-Hope, and Captain Experience, and cut, wounded, and pierced them so dreadfully that, what with discouragement, what with disorder, and what with the wounds they had received and the loss of much blood, they could barely get back safe into the stronghold, though for strength they were the three best hands in Mansoul.

When the main body of the Prince’s army saw how badly these three captains had fared, they made as safe and orderly a retreat as they could, back in by the sally-port; and that was the end of this action. But Diabolus was so flushed with this night’s work that he promised himself an easy and complete conquest of the town of Mansoul within a few days. So the next day he came up to its walls with great boldness and demanded entrance, and that they surrender themselves to his government at once. The Diabolonians within, too, began to grow somewhat lively, as we will show later.

But the valiant Lord Mayor replied that whatever he got he must get by force; for as long as Emmanuel their Prince was alive (though for the present he was not with them as they wished), they would never consent to yield Mansoul up to another.

And with that Lord Willbewill stood up and said, “Diabolus, master of the den and enemy of all that is good, we poor inhabitants of the town of Mansoul know your rule and government too well, and the end that will certainly follow if we submit to you, to do it. While we were without knowledge we let you take us, as the bird that did not see the snare fell into the hands of the fowler. But since then we have been turned from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God. [Acts 26:18] And though by your cunning, and the cunning of the Diabolonians within, we have suffered great loss and plunged ourselves into great perplexity, yet give ourselves up, lay down our arms, and yield to so horrible a tyrant as you, we will not. We would rather die where we stand. Besides, we have hope that in time deliverance will come to us from the court, and so we will keep up the war against you.”

This brave speech of Lord Willbewill’s, together with the Lord Mayor’s, somewhat checked the boldness of Diabolus, though it kindled the fury of his rage. It also heartened the townsmen and captains; indeed, it was like a healing plaster on brave Captain Credence’s wound. For you must understand that a brave speech just then was timely and of great service, when the captains had come home routed and the enemy, emboldened by his success, had drawn up to the walls and demanded entrance.

Lord Willbewill also played the man within. For while the captains and soldiers were in the field, he was in arms in the town; and wherever he found a Diabolonian, that one was made to feel the weight of his heavy hand and the edge of his piercing sword. So he wounded many of the Diabolonians, such as Lord Cavil, Lord Brisk, Lord Meddler, and Lord Murmur, and he badly maimed several of the lesser sort, though I cannot at this time give you an account of any that he killed outright. He had this opening because the captains had gone out to fight the enemy in the field. “For now,” thought the Diabolonians within, “is our time to stir and raise an uproar in the town.” So what did they do but quickly gather themselves into a body and fall at once to storming through Mansoul like a hurricane, as if there would now be nothing there but whirlwind and tempest? So, as I said, he took this opportunity to fall on them with his men, cutting and slashing with undaunted courage; at which the Diabolonians scattered in all haste to their hiding places, and my lord returned to his post as before.

This brave act of my lord’s somewhat avenged the wrong Diabolus had done to the captains, and also let them know that Mansoul was not to be given up for the loss of a victory or two. So the tyrant’s wing was clipped again as far as boasting went; I mean, in comparison with what he would have done if the Diabolonians had put the town in the same plight he had put the captains in.
